passage.title: Racing the Rumbling Earth
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Deep beneath the ground we walk on, giant slabs of rock press tightly against each other along cracks called faults. For years, rough edges lock these rocks in place while stress builds up. When the rock finally snaps and slips, a burst of stored energy races out in all directions. We feel this sudden shaking on the surface as an earthquake. Yet an earthquake does not travel as one single jolt. Instead, it sends out two main waves that move at very different speeds.

The fastest runner in this underground race is the primary wave, or P-wave. Like a sound wave moving through air, a P-wave pushes and pulls solid rock straight forward and back. Because it squeezes rock in a straight line, it travels nearly four miles per second through Earth's crust. Dogs often bark and window glass rattles when this first pulse passes under a town. Still, P-waves rarely knock down walls or crack roads. They feel more like a quick tap on the floor.

Several seconds later, the slower secondary wave, or S-wave, arrives at the same spot. Traveling at roughly half the speed of the first pulse, an S-wave shakes the ground from side to side and up and down like a snapped rope. This rolling motion twists building frames and shifts heavy bridges. Consequently, most bad damage during an earthquake happens after the S-wave hits.

Scientists use the gap between these two waves to build early warning networks. Inside a buried station, a heavy metal weight hangs from a strong spring above a recorder. When the fast P-wave strikes the vault, the outer frame shakes while the heavy hanging weight stays still. Faint ground tremors from the early P-wave, detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors, are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers. Because radio and fiber-optic signals travel at the speed of light, the computer message outruns the slower S-wave.

Even ten to thirty seconds of early warning can save many lives. Automatic switches slow down high-speed trains so they do not derail. Doctors in hospitals pause delicate work, and fire station doors roll open before the frame can jam. While scientists cannot stop faults from slipping, reading the first wave gives towns time to brace for the second.

tier2Words.definition: a single short burst or beat of energy moving through a space
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root pellere ('to push or beat')
tier2Words.contextClue: When this first burst of wave energy passes under a town, windowpanes rattle before the second wave arrives.

tier2Words.definition: as a result or outcome of what just happened
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root sequi ('to follow') + prefix con- ('with')
tier2Words.contextClue: Because an S-wave twists building frames and shifts bridges, most serious damage happens as a result.

tier2Words.definition: slight quivering or shaking movements of the ground
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root tremere ('to shake or tremble')
tier2Words.contextClue: Buried sensors detect the faint shaking caused by the early P-wave before the stronger S-wave arrives.

tier2Words.definition: to run off the metal tracks
tier2Words.rootHint: Prefix de- ('off, away from') + rail ('metal track')
tier2Words.contextClue: Automatic switches slow down high-speed trains before the shaking ground can throw them off the tracks.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Faint ground tremors from the early P-wave, detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors, are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers."

Based on the sentence, what detects the faint ground tremors, and what turns them into warning alerts?

options.text: Fast computers detect the faults underground, and buried seismic sensors send out radio alerts.
Buried seismic sensors detect the faint ground tremors, and fast computers turn them into warning alerts.
The early P-wave turns the buried seismic sensors into fast computers near the city.
Barking dogs detect the S-wave first, and train drivers phone the fire stations.

questions.provingSentenceText: Faint ground tremors from the early P-wave, detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors, are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers.
questions.childTip: Look at both 'by' phrases: buried seismic sensors detect the tremors, and fast computers turn them into alerts.
questions.parentExplanation: This passive sentence features two 'by' phrases: 'detected... by buried seismic sensors' and 'are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers'. Option B correctly identifies both agents.

"Faint ground tremors from the early P-wave, detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors, are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers."

What does the word tremors mean as it is used in Paragraph 4?

options.text: Deep underground caves filled with water
Loud sirens mounted on the roofs of fire stations
Heavy metal weights that never move at all
Slight shaking or vibrating movements in the earth

questions.provingSentenceText: Faint ground tremors from the early P-wave, detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors, are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers.
questions.childTip: Connect 'ground tremors' to what the early P-wave does as it passes through the earth.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 4, 'faint ground tremors from the early P-wave' refers to the mild shaking vibrations detected by buried seismic sensors.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, why do S-waves cause much more damage to buildings and bridges than P-waves?

options.text: They shake the ground side to side and up and down, which twists building frames.
They travel twice as fast as P-waves and arrive before sensors can turn on.
They cut the fiber-optic cables that connect hospitals to fire stations.
They melt the solid rock deep beneath the fault into hot liquid lava.

questions.provingSentenceText: Traveling at roughly half the speed of the first pulse, an S-wave shakes the ground from side to side and up and down like a snapped rope.
questions.childTip: Click the sentence in Paragraph 3 that compares the S-wave's movement to a snapped rope.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 explains that S-waves shake the ground side to side and up and down like a snapped rope, a rolling motion that twists building frames and shifts heavy bridges.

questions.prompt: How does the author organize the information in Paragraphs 2 and 3?

options.text: By explaining step by step how engineers pour concrete for highway bridges
By listing the dates of the ten largest earthquakes in United States history
By comparing the speed, motion, and impact of P-waves and S-waves
By arguing that buried seismic sensors are too expensive for small towns to use

questions.provingSentenceText: Several seconds later, the slower secondary wave, or S-wave, arrives at the same spot.
questions.childTip: Look at how Paragraph 2 describes the fast P-wave while Paragraph 3 contrasts it with the slower S-wave.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 use a comparison/contrast and sequence structure to contrast the fast, mild, straight-line P-wave with the slower, destructive, rolling S-wave.

questions.prompt: Part A: Based on the passage, why is an earthquake warning system able to alert a city before the dangerous shaking begins?

options.text: Satellites in space can see underground faults glowing red a full week before an earthquake starts.
Heavy metal weights inside the fault stop the rocks from slipping until trains have come to a full stop.
S-waves travel much faster than radio signals, giving computers several hours to predict the storm.
Sensors detect the harmless P-wave first and send light-speed computer signals that arrive ahead of the slower S-wave.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because radio and fiber-optic signals travel at the speed of light, the computer message outruns the slower S-wave.
questions.childTip: Check Paragraph 4 to see how the computer message wins the race against the slower S-wave.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 explains that buried sensors detect the fast P-wave first, and because radio and fiber-optic signals move at the speed of light, the warning alert outruns the slower, destructive S-wave.
